entries.title: 4-year-old in critical condition after being shot in the head
entries.summary: <p>A 4-year-old boy is in critical condition after he was shot in the head in South Deering Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Officers responded to a residence in the 2200 block of East 99th Street at 4:01 p.m. and found the boy, police said. He was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody and an investigation is ongoing into the incident, police said. </p>

entries.title: White Sox anticipating raucous crowd, seek to clinch first postseason-series victory at home since 1906
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> played their last home game a week and a half ago.</p><p>They fended off the Rockies and were cheered for a successful regular season that resulted in their highest home attendance in four years (1.986 million). For a marquee MLB franchise, that figure might represent a crisis. But it was well above the threshold where the Sox felt supported.</p><p>‘‘The most simple way to put what is special about our club is the enthusiasm on the field,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘When you’re a player and there’s no one in the stands, you kind of question who you are. When you’re on the field and there’s a bunch of people there, that gives you confidence that you’re a good club that people are paying good money to come see.’’</p><p>But as the sixth seed in the American League playoffs, the Sox left town last week not knowing whether they would play in Chicago again this year. It was an irksome notion.</p><p>‘‘Our fans, they deserve baseball in October,’’ All-Star third baseman Miguel Vargas said.</p><p>Vargas is one of the few players on hand who has observed the Sox’ progression from the losingest MLB team of all time in 2024 to a team a victory away from reaching the AL Championship Series next week. There has been enough turnover for this to feel like an entirely new project.</p><p>‘‘There is a big change in personnel; this is a very, very different team,’’ said right-hander Erick Fedde, who was also on the 2024 club. ‘‘A lot of new faces to create the success.’’</p><p>Surely, there has been a new crop of viewers drawn to a team that socked 211 home runs this season and produces at least one viral video clip per week. By and large, however, the Sox’ fan base simply has endured the wait for meaningful baseball.</p><p>For that reason, ensuring a home playoff game was a rallying cry for the Sox, something celebrated in the locker room in Houston after a sweep of the wild-card series.</p><p>‘‘We’re expecting the most rowdy crowd I’ve ever played before in my entire life,’’ said right-hander Sean Burke, who made his big-league debut in 2024.</p><p>With the Sox’ two victories in Cleveland, however, the scale of potential happenings this week at Rate Field has increased again.</p><p>The 2005 Sox clinched all three of their playoff-series victories, as well as their division title, on the road. When the 1959 Sox clinched the AL pennant, prompting Chicago Fire Commissioner Robert Quinn to turn on the air-raid sirens, the team was in Cleveland. That might explain why so many people were startled. No Sox team has locked down the final victory of a playoff series in front of its home fans since the club won the World Series in 1906.</p><p>‘‘One hundred twenty years?’’ surprised reliever Grant Taylor said. ‘‘Maybe we can do it this year.’’</p><p>Maybe a historic release of fan energy is the key ingredient. By the admission of the players and coaches, the Sox have been more comfortable as an underdog than as a front-runner. A slate of road playoff games as the lower seed found them back in a comfortable mindset. They could use an extra jolt.</p><p>‘‘That is definitely true that we have a lot of comfort in being the underdog; that is the story of this club,’’ Venable said. ‘‘I don’t think any of it matters. We get to play a playoff game at home, and that’s all these guys are really thinking about.’’</p><p>While the 20-somethings on the roster might be light on their franchise history, they know the environment that awaits them doesn’t come easily or often.</p><p>‘‘This could be a once-in-a-lifetime thing for us,’’ outfielder Tristan Peters said. ‘‘You’ve got to be excited.’’</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/chicago-white-sox-rivals-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-stephen-vogt-sam-antonacci-sean-newcomb-jordan-hicks-brewers-tigers-twins-bulls-cavaliers" >White Sox need a rival, and Guardians fit the bill — they just have to dislike each other</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/white-sox-have-leaned-into-their-strengths-will-heavy-bullpen-use-but-change-is-coming-will-venable-chris-getz-erick-fedde-sean-newcomb-sean-burke-munetaka-murakami" >White Sox have leaned into strengths with heavy bullpen use, but change is coming</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man sentenced to 15 years for selling gun to undercover cop used in fatal shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man has been sentenced to 15 years in federal prison for selling an undercover Chicago police officer a gun he had used to fatally shoot a man in Greater Grand Crossing, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Levion Thomas was sentenced last Thursday by U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin after pleading guilty to a federal illegal firearm possession charge in 2024, according to the federal office.</p><p>The gun Thomas possessed had been tied to the murder of Troy Pouncey, 31, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/3/5/23626332/man-shot-to-death-greater-grand-crossing" target="_blank" ><u>shot</u></a> in his face and body around 1:15 p.m. in the 7100 block of South Calumet Avenue March 5, 2023, according to Chicago police. He was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where he later died.</p><p>The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, along with Chicago police, arranged for a purchase of the weapon by an undercover officer after finding Thomas had been looking to sell the weapon, prosecutors said in court documents.</p><p>Thomas sold the gun, which he used to kill Pouncey, to an undercover Chicago police officer in the front seat of a car in Burnham, Illinois, 15 days after the shooting.</p><p>Thomas initially got into the vehicle wearing a mask before removing it, which revealed his face to the cameras inside the car. He then took $500 in exchange for the handgun, per court documents. Thomas had previously pleaded guilty to a charge of aggravated unlawful use of a weapon in 2021, for which he was sentenced to a year in prison.</p><p>“Too many people in this city believe that they can unlawfully possess firearms with impunity,” Assistant U.S. Attorneys Julia Schwartz and Jessica Ecker wrote in court documents. “This needs to stop.”</p>

entries.title: Sales surge for businesses near Rate Field as White Sox gears up for Game 3
entries.summary: <p>A line of more than 20 customers stood outside of sports retail store Grandstand before it opened Tuesday at 10 a.m, but co-owners Josh and Stephanie Ganal weren't surprised. </p><p>The store at 600 W. 35th St., a few blocks from Rate Field, has been flooded with enthusiastic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> fans for weeks. And business has ramped up even more ahead of Wednesday's Game 3 of the American League Division Series.</p><p>If the Sox win, it would be their first time in the American League Championship Series since 2005.</p><p>Businesses near Rate Field, like Grandstand, have seen record foot traffic and sales, along with a joyful mob of fans.</p><p>“It’s very similar [to 2005],” Josh Ganal said of the excitement. “I think the only difference is that time we were expected to be there. This time, it's exciting to be there.”</p><p>The last few seasons have been tough for the Sox, with three years of at least 100 losses, plus an MLB record of 121 losses in 2024.</p><p>“Nobody was really expecting this team to come out as good as they are,” Josh Ganal said. “It's a different team entirely. They’re fun to watch. You can't ever count them out, and it's good for the city. It rejuvenates a totally different era of fans.”</p><p>He said this year's team roster is full of personality and camaraderie.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Benet's Gene Heidkamp tops our list of high school basketball coaching awards
entries.summary: <p>With local high school boys basketball coaches a month away from welcoming their teams back into the gym to start practicing for the upcoming season, here’s a look at who could be considered the best among them in several categories:</p><h3><b>Best coach: Gene Heidkamp, Benet</b></h3><h3></h3><p>It’s hard to look at Heidkamp’s 18 years at Benet and argue for anyone else. Benet basketball has a profound identity, credited largely to a coach held in the highest respect by colleagues and counterparts.</p><p>There’s also the obvious: results.</p><p>Heidkamp has built arguably the best program in the state — a model of consistency with a winning percentage of 74% over nearly two decades. His Redwings brought home a state championship in March 2025 after runner-up finishes in 2014, 2016, 2023, and were runners-up again last season.</p><h3><b>Best coach without a state title: Mike Ellis, Evanston</b></h3><h3></h3><p>In 23 years, Ellis has accumulated more than 500 career victories while leading two powerhouses in Peoria Richwoods and Evanston. He has done everything but win a state title, although he has been close with five state tournament appearances, including runner-up finishes in 2006 and 2010 with Richwoods and 2019 with Evanston, as well as eight sectional championships.</p><p>His Wildkits have the potential to capture another trophy in Champaign in March, possibly taking Ellis off the list of those who’ve never won the big one.</p><h3><b>Most overlooked coach: Tom Livatino, Loyola</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Only true high school hoops junkies are likely to know the Ramblers have averaged 23 victories a year in their last 13 full seasons under Livatino. They’ve picked up eight regional titles in that time, as well as a sectional title in 2014. Their 30-4 team in 2019-20, arguably Livatino’s best, was set to play for a sectional title before the COVID-19 pandemic shut every-thing down. Livatino also averaged 20 wins a season in five seasons at Lincoln Park, where the Lions won three regional titles.</p><p>Still, perhaps the strongest indicator of Livatino’s impact is that opponents hate the tough, defensive-minded grind they have to deal with when playing Loyola.</p><h3><b>Most consistent head coach: Mike Oliver, Curie</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Oliver has built quite the résumé with the Condors, leading them to a Class 4A title in 2016 and three city championships, the last in 2024. Although many of their achievements aren’t appreciated enough outside the city, the long history of success can’t be denied. Perhaps no coach in the state has won as consistently for as long as Oliver has, building a<br>578-176 record in 30-plus years. It isn’t just about the win totals, either — the consistency also applies to his style and approach, the type of players on his teams and the expectations of his program.</p><h3><b>Most underrated coach: Eric Millstone</b></h3><h3></h3><p>There were some lean years after Millstone first started at Palatine, but he has quietly and clearly put his stamp on the program over 18 seasons by instilling discipline, maximizing talent and implementing a defensive scheme that has transformed the Pirates into an effective force.</p><p>Over the last five seasons, Palatine has averaged 24 wins. They had a breakthrough in 2024 with an appearance in Champaign, where they finished fourth in the state tournament in Class 4A. They also won a school-record 29 games last season.</p>
